claim: The human kinome is encoded by more than 500 genes.
source: The human kinome is encoded by more than 500 genes which lead to the synthesis of functionally diverse kinases.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature about the human kinome.

claim: All kinases contain a structurally conserved phosphotransferase domain.
source: Kinases are different in their domain composition but all contain a structurally conserved phosphotransferase domain (Manning, 2009, Kornev and Taylor, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Manning, 2009 and Kornev and Taylor, 2010.

claim: Protein kinases regulate various aspects of cellular functions including cell survival, apoptosis, cell division, and metabolism via reversible and tightly regulated phosphorylations.
source: Protein kinases regulate various aspects of cellular functions including cell survival, apoptosis, cell division, and metabolism via reversible and tightly regulated phosphorylations (Figure 1A; Bhullar et al., 2018, Blume-Jensen and Hunter, 2001, Manning et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bhullar et al., 2018, Blume-Jensen and Hunter, 2001, and Manning et al., 2002, and referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: Kinase domains display scaffolding functions in addition to kinase phosphotransferase activities.
source: In addition to kinase phosphotransferase activities, kinase domains display scaffolding functions (Shrestha et al., 2020, Reiterer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shrestha et al., 2020 and Reiterer et al., 2014.

claim: Kinases act as molecular switches, adopting conformational states that align with an active (ON) or inactive (OFF) kinase state.
source: On the cellular level, kinases act as molecular switches, adopting conformational states that align with an active (ON) or inactive (OFF) kinase state (Huse and Kuriyan, 2002, Yamaguchi and Hendrickson, 1996, Lopez et al., 2020, Feichtner et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Huse and Kuriyan, 2002, Yamaguchi and Hendrickson, 1996, Lopez et al., 2020, and Feichtner et al., 2022.

claim: The activity of a kinase can be altered by post-translational modifications (PTMs) of selected amino acids.
source: First, the activity of a kinase can be altered by post-translational modifications (PTMs) of selected amino acids. PTMs alter kinase characteristics like its activity status, its location within the cell, rate of degradation, and its associations with other proteins (Chou, 2020, Cohen, 2000, Deribe et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chou, 2020, Cohen, 2000, and Deribe et al., 2010.

claim: PTMs alter kinase characteristics like its activity status, its location within the cell, rate of degradation, and its associations with other proteins.
source: PTMs alter kinase characteristics like its activity status, its location within the cell, rate of degradation, and its associations with other proteins (Chou, 2020, Cohen, 2000, Deribe et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chou, 2020, Cohen, 2000, and Deribe et al., 2010.

claim: Scaffolding functions of kinase domains play central roles in the activation and deactivation process of interacting kinase protomers.
source: Second, the scaffolding functions of kinase domains accompany the process of phosphotransferase reactions. These play central roles in the activation and deactivation process of interacting kinase protomers.
evidence: This is a statement about the role of scaffolding functions based on the authors' interpretation of the literature.

claim: Scaffolding functions are key for pseudokinase activities, for relaying signaling inputs without catalytic functions.
source: This feature is key for pseudokinase activities, for relaying signaling inputs without catalytic functions (Weinlich and Green, 2014, Morrison and Davis, 2003, Boudeau et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Weinlich and Green, 2014, Morrison and Davis, 2003, and Boudeau et al., 2006.

claim: Intramolecular auto-inhibitory modules (AIMs) alter kinase activity states by reducing the accessibility of the substrate protein for the subsequent kiss-and-run phosphotransferase reaction.
source: Intramolecular auto-inhibitory modules (AIMs) alter kinase activity states by reducing the accessibility of the substrate protein for the subsequent kiss-and-run phosphotransferase reaction (Mayrhofer et al., 2020, Pufall and Graves, 2002, Xu et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mayrhofer et al., 2020, Pufall and Graves, 2002, and Xu et al., 2002.

claim: Kinase domain activities are controlled through inter- or intramolecular interactions with substrate-like sequences in some cases.
source: In some cases, kinase domain activities are controlled through inter- or intramolecular interactions with substrate-like sequences.
evidence: This is a general statement about kinase regulation mechanisms.

claim: Pseudo-substrate stretches bind to the catalytic cleft of the kinase and hinder the phosphorylation of the substrate.
source: Pseudo-substrate stretches bind to the catalytic cleft of the kinase and hinder the phosphorylation of the substrate. This binding to the catalytic site is altered in response to input signals and manifested in kinase conformational changes, which in turn coordinate protein kinase activation cycles (Schmitt et al., 2022, Kemp et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schmitt et al., 2022 and Kemp et al., 1994.

claim: Activating and inactivating regulatory protein interactions exist and have been described for prototypical kinases such as PKA and CDKs.
source: Besides intramolecular inhibition both activating and inactivating regulatory protein interactions exist and have been described for prototypical kinases such as PKA and CDKs (Boudeau et al., 2003, Taylor et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boudeau et al., 2003 and Taylor et al., 2005.

claim: Kinase regulation is strongly dependent on the expression pattern and how the protein is stabilized in regard to the cell fate within the respective cell system or compartment.
source: Fourth, kinase regulation is strongly dependent on the expression pattern and how the protein is stabilized in regard to the cell fate within the respective cell system or compartment (Capra et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Capra et al., 2006.

claim: Regulatory protein interactions of kinases depend on small molecule interactions.
source: Fifth, regulatory protein interactions of kinases depend on small molecule interactions. Besides different types of second messengers (e.g. Ca2+, IP3, cAMP) (Newton et al., 2016, Kasai and Petersen, 1994) a collection of metabolites and ions contribute in orchestrating cellular kinase functions (Ramms et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Newton et al., 2016, Kasai and Petersen, 1994, and Ramms et al., 2021.

claim: Deregulation of kinase functions is associated with the development of numerous diseases, such as cancer, inflammatory, infectious, and degenerative conditions.
source: Alterations of the ON and OFF states of kinases are also pertinent to kinase-related disorders. Deregulation of kinase functions is associated with the development of numerous diseases, such as cancer, inflammatory, infectious, and degenerative conditions (Shchemelinin et al., 2006, Köstler and Zielinski, 2015, Ferguson and Gray, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shchemelinin et al., 2006, Köstler and Zielinski, 2015, and Ferguson and Gray, 2018.

claim: Kinase malfunctions result from gene mutations, deletions, fusions, or increased or aberrant expressions.
source: Kinase malfunctions result from gene mutations, deletions, fusions, or increased or aberrant expressions. These mechanisms result in gain or loss of function of the involved kinase pathways, thus driving disease etiology and progression (Ochoa et al., 2018, Van et al., 2021, Cicenas et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ochoa et al., 2018, Van et al., 2021, and Cicenas et al., 2018.

claim: LKB1 is active as trimeric cytoplasmic protein complex.
source: LKB1 is active as trimeric cytoplasmic protein complex.
evidence: This is a statement about LKB1 function.

claim: LKB1 is the upstream regulator of the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK).
source: It is the upstream regulator of the AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) (Rodríguez et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodríguez et al., 2021.

claim: LKB1 promotes AMPK signaling by forming an heterotrimeric complex with the pseudokinase STE20-related adaptor alpha (STRADα) and the scaffolding protein Mouse protein-25 (MO25) through phosphorylation and thus activation of cytoplasmic AMPK.
source: LKB1 promotes AMPK signaling by forming an heterotrimeric complex with the pseudokinase STE20-related adaptor alpha (STRADα) and the scaffolding protein Mouse protein-25 (MO25) through phosphorylation and thus activation of cytoplasmic AMPK (Boudeau et al., 2004, Narbonne et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boudeau et al., 2004 and Narbonne et al., 2010.

claim: Mutations in LKB1 can lead to the autosomal dominant disease Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS).
source: Mutations in LKB1 can lead to the autosomal dominant disease Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) (Mehenni et al., 1998, Beggs et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mehenni et al., 1998 and Beggs et al., 2010.

claim: Inactivating mutations of LKB1 are frequently observed in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), cervical carcinoma, and malignant melanoma.
source: Inactivating mutations of LKB1 are frequently observed in non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), cervical carcinoma, and malignant melanoma (Wingo et al., 2009, Ndembe et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wingo et al., 2009 and Ndembe et al., 2022.

claim: RIPK1 acts as a central stress sensor to control cell survival, inflammation, and cell death signaling.
source: RIPK1 acts as a central stress sensor to control cell survival, inflammation, and cell death signaling (Clucas and Meier, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clucas and Meier, 2023.

claim: Deregulation of RIPK1- and RIPK3-involved signaling cascades have been linked to inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, autoimmune conditions, and neuroinflammatory diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.
source: Deregulation of RIPK1- and RIPK3-involved signaling cascades have been linked to inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, autoimmune conditions, and neuroinflammatory diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease (Martens et al., 2020, Li et al., 2019, Speir et al., 2021, Clucas and Meier, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Martens et al., 2020, Li et al., 2019, Speir et al., 2021, and Clucas and Meier, 2023.

claim: RIPK1 and RIPK3 may share a similar mechanism of action with BRAF, as their structural arrangements and the dimerization of their kinase domains bear resemblance.
source: It's intriguing to note that RIPK1 and RIPK3 may share a similar mechanism of action with BRAF, as their structural arrangements and the dimerization of their kinase domains bear resemblance (Raju et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raju et al., 2018.

claim: Auto-phosphorylation of RIPK1 and RIPK3 represents a central regulatory element.
source: In addition to this, auto-phosphorylation of RIPK1 and RIPK3 represents a central regulatory element, overall showing some similar molecular ties to BRAF (Laurien et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Laurien et al., 2020.

claim: The central role of CDK4/6 lies in regulating cell cycle progression by phosphorylating and activating the key substrate retinoblastoma protein (Rb) that promotes G1 to S phase transition.
source: The central role of CDK4/6 lies in regulating cell cycle progression by phosphorylating and activating the key substrate retinoblastoma protein (Rb) that promotes G1 to S phase transition.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about CDK4/6 function.

claim: CDK4/6 regulation is controlled by complex formation with regulatory polypeptides.
source: On the molecular level this is controlled by complex formation of CDK4 and CDK6 with regulatory polypeptides (James et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to James et al., 2008.

claim: Binding to p16INK4a blocks CDK4/6 functions.
source: Binding to p16INK4a, one of the most frequently mutated tumor suppressor proteins, blocks CDK4/6 functions (Quelle et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quelle et al., 1997.

claim: p16INK4a is one of the most frequently mutated tumor suppressor proteins.
source: Binding to p16INK4a, one of the most frequently mutated tumor suppressor proteins, blocks CDK4/6 functions (Quelle et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citation to Quelle et al., 1997.

claim: Cancer mutations in p16INK4a counteract the blocking of CDK4/6 functions.
source: Cancer mutations in p16INK4a counteract this.
evidence: This is inferred from the context about p16INK4a mutations and CDK4/6 regulation.

claim: Kinase activating cyclinD proteins bind to CDK4/6 to promote carcinogenesis.
source: As a result, kinase activating cyclinD proteins bind to CDK4/6 to promote carcinogenesis (VanArsdale et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to VanArsdale et al., 2015.

claim: CDK4/6 inhibitors found the way into the clinic, in particular for treating breast cancer patients.
source: Thus, CDK4/6 inhibitors (CDK4/6i) found the way into the clinic, in particular for treating breast cancer patients (Nebenfuehr et al., 2020; Yu et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nebenfuehr et al., 2020 and Yu et al., 2006.

claim: The development of drug resistance upon CDK4/6 inhibitor therapies underscores the need for personalized treatments that consider the patient's genetic profile and the underlying alterations of CDK4/6 complexes present in their cancer cells.
source: The development of drug resistance upon CDK4/6 inhibitor therapies underscores the need for personalized treatments that consider the patient's genetic profile and the underlying alterations of CDK4/6 complexes present in their cancer cells (Álvarez-Fernández and Malumbres, 2020, Knudsen and Witkiewicz, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Álvarez-Fernández and Malumbres, 2020 and Knudsen and Witkiewicz, 2017.

claim: Conventional methods often fall short in capturing the dynamics of kinase phosphotransferase and scaffolding activities which occur in their native cellular environments.
source: Conventional methods often fall short in capturing the dynamics of kinase phosphotransferase and scaffolding activities which occur in their native cellular environments (Klaeger et al., 2017, Croce et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klaeger et al., 2017 and Croce et al., 2019.

claim: At expression levels far below the endogenous kinase, protein activity conformations can be tracked in intact cells using the KinCon reporter.
source: These data underline that at expression levels far below the endogenous kinase, protein activity conformations can be tracked in intact cells.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: 1 hr of PLX8394 drug exposure exclusively converted BRAF-V600E to the more closed conformation at expression levels of the BRAF KinCon reporter below the immunoblotting detection limit.
source: Using this readout, we showed that at expression levels of the BRAF KinCon reporter below the immunoblotting detection limit, 1 hr of drug exposure exclusively converted BRAF-V600E to the more closed conformation (Figure 1F and G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The pseudokinase domain of STRADα directly interacts with the kinase domain of LKB1, thus triggering the activation of LKB1's tumor-suppressing phosphotransferase functions.
source: The pseudokinase domain of STRADα directly interacts with the kinase domain of LKB1, thus triggering the activation of LKB1's tumor-suppressing phosphotransferase functions (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: Referenced in Figure 2B and C.

claim: Upon ATP-binding STRADα occupies an active conformation.
source: It is assumed that upon ATP-binding STRADα occupies an active conformation.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption based on existing knowledge.

claim: In the scenario where STRADα occupies an active conformation, LKB1 affinities for binding rise and it binds as a pseudo-substrate.
source: In this scenario LKB1 affinities for binding rise and it binds as a pseudo-substrate.
evidence: This is part of the mechanistic explanation of LKB1-STRADα interaction.

claim: MO25 acts as scaffold for the kinase dimer to promote the activated LKB1 conformation state.
source: MO25 acts as scaffold for the kinase dimer to promote the activated LKB1 conformation state (Zeqiraj et al., 2009a, Zeqiraj et al., 2009b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zeqiraj et al., 2009a and Zeqiraj et al., 2009b.

claim: MO25 binding stabilizes the trimeric cytoplasmic LKB1-STRADα-MO25 complex.
source: Further, MO25 binding stabilizes this trimeric cytoplasmic complex (Figure 2A and B; Boudeau et al., 2003, Baas et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Boudeau et al., 2003 and Baas et al., 2003, and referenced in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The highest increase of LKB1-mediated downstream phosphorylation of AMPKα-T172 was observed following co-expression of both MO25 and STRADα.
source: Next, we employed the pT172-AMPK/AMPK ratio as a measure of cellular LKB1 activity, observing the highest increase of LKB1-mediated downstream phosphorylation of AMPKα-T172 following co-expression of both, MO25 and STRADα, respectively.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from co-expression experiments.

claim: A similar effect on AMPK phosphorylation was observed when solely over-expressing STRADα using the chosen cellular setting and transfection protocol with a 1:1:1 ratio of transfected expression constructs.
source: Using the chosen cellular setting and transfection protocol with a 1:1:1 ratio of transfected expression constructs, a similar effect was observed when solely over-expressing STRADα.
evidence: This is based on experimental data from co-expression experiments.

claim: No impact on AMPK phosphorylation was observed when MO25 was coexpressed alone.
source: No impact on AMPK phosphorylation was observed when MO25 was coexpressed alone (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only faint STRADα KinCon signals were detected in the absence of MO25 and LKB1 co-expression.
source: Notable is the fact that only faint STRADα KinCon signals were detected in the absence of MO25 and LKB1 co-expression.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: A more than 10-fold elevation of the STRADα KinCon reporter signals was observed following co-expression of both LKB1 and MO25 interacting partners in HEK293T cells (48 hr of expression).
source: To our surprise we have observed a more than 10-fold elevation of the reporter signals following co-expression of both interacting partners in HEK293T cells (48 hr of expression, Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: STRADα engages an opened conformation where C and N termini are separated and thus almost no bioluminescence signals can be detected under basal conditions.
source: This data supports the notion that STRADα engages an opened conformation, where C and N termini are separated and thus almost no bioluminescence signals can be detected under basal conditions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Upon interaction with LKB1, STRADα conformation shifts to a partially closed intermediate state.
source: Upon interaction with LKB1 this conformation shifts to a partially closed intermediate state.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The trimeric complex further promotes STRADα structure closing.
source: The trimeric complex further promotes structure closing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The STRADα-H231A/F233A (HF) mutations prevent STRADα-LKB1 dimer and greatly hinders STRADα-MO25-LKB1 trimer formation and thereby AMPK activation.
source: It has previously been reported that these mutations prevent STRADα-LKB1 dimer and greatly hinders STRADα-MO25-LKB1 trimer formation and thereby AMPK activation (Zeqiraj et al., 2009a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeqiraj et al., 2009a.

claim: The HF double mutation of STRADα is sufficient to abolish the elevating effect of trimer complex formation on the LKB1 KinCon reporter.
source: We observed that the so-called HF double mutation of STRADα is sufficient to abolish the elevating effect of trimer complex formation (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Both H231A and F233A mutations are located in the LKB1/STRADα binding interface, thereby preventing complex formation.
source: Indeed both mutations are located in the LKB1/STRADα binding interface, thereby preventing complex formation (Qing et al., 2022, Zeqiraj et al., 2009a; Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by citations to Qing et al., 2022 and Zeqiraj et al., 2009a, and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Trimeric complex formation alters the opening and closing of the tested full-length kinase structures using the applied KinCon reporter readout.
source: These findings underline that trimeric complex formation alters the opening and closing of the tested full-length kinase structures using the applied KinCon reporter readout.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: LKB1 loss-of-function mutations have been identified in a plethora of pathological conditions including autosomal diseases and many different forms of cancers.
source: LKB1 loss-of-function mutations have been identified in a plethora of pathological conditions including autosomal diseases and many different forms of cancers (Sanchez-Cespedes, 2007, Launonen, 2005, Molaei et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sanchez-Cespedes, 2007, Launonen, 2005, and Molaei et al., 2022.

claim: K78 forms a salt bridge with E98 on the αC-helix which stabilizes a functional active conformation of LKB1.
source: K78 forms a salt bridge with E98 on the αC-helix which stabilizes a functional active conformation, the catalytic D176 is crucial for phosphoryl transfer, and D194 is part of the DFG motif involved in binding of the Mg2+ ion (Fabbro et al., 2015, Meharena et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fabbro et al., 2015 and Meharena et al., 2016.

claim: The catalytic D176 is crucial for phosphoryl transfer in LKB1.
source: K78 forms a salt bridge with E98 on the αC-helix which stabilizes a functional active conformation, the catalytic D176 is crucial for phosphoryl transfer, and D194 is part of the DFG motif involved in binding of the Mg2+ ion (Fabbro et al., 2015, Meharena et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fabbro et al., 2015 and Meharena et al., 2016.

claim: D194 is part of the DFG motif involved in binding of the Mg2+ ion in LKB1.
source: K78 forms a salt bridge with E98 on the αC-helix which stabilizes a functional active conformation, the catalytic D176 is crucial for phosphoryl transfer, and D194 is part of the DFG motif involved in binding of the Mg2+ ion (Fabbro et al., 2015, Meharena et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fabbro et al., 2015 and Meharena et al., 2016.

claim: The residue W308 is part of a hydrophobic cluster and thus surrounded by lipophilic residues in LKB1.
source: The residue W308 is part of a hydrophobic cluster and thus surrounded by lipophilic residues (Zeqiraj et al., 2009a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeqiraj et al., 2009a.

claim: R74 is located within the STRADα binding interface, and has been reported to interact with STRADα-Q251.
source: R74 is located within the STRADα binding interface, and has been reported to interact with STRADα-Q251 (Zeqiraj et al., 2009a), and K48 is a solvent-exposed acetylation site (Zubiete-Franco et al., 2019, Zeqiraj et al., 2009a) located on the back of the N-lobe.
evidence: Supported by citations to Zeqiraj et al., 2009a and Zubiete-Franco et al., 2019.

claim: K48 is a solvent-exposed acetylation site located on the back of the N-lobe of LKB1.
source: R74 is located within the STRADα binding interface, and has been reported to interact with STRADα-Q251 (Zeqiraj et al., 2009a), and K48 is a solvent-exposed acetylation site (Zubiete-Franco et al., 2019, Zeqiraj et al., 2009a) located on the back of the N-lobe.
evidence: Supported by citations to Zubiete-Franco et al., 2019 and Zeqiraj et al., 2009a.

claim: Only the W308C mutation prevented significant closing of the LKB1 conformation when co-expressed with STRADα and MO25.
source: Among these mutations, only the W308C mutation prevented significant closing of the LKB1 conformation when co-expressed with STRADα and MO25 (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The catalytic site residues are critical for enzymatic activity, but play a less important role in maintaining the active LKB1 conformation in the presence of both STRADα and MO25.
source: This indicates that the catalytic site residues are critical for enzymatic activity, but play a less important role in maintaining the active LKB1 conformation in the presence of both STRADα and MO25.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The W308C mutation has previously been identified to cause a reduction in LKB1 stability when compared to the wt variant.
source: The W308C mutation has previously been identified to cause a reduction in LKB1 stability when compared to the wt variant (Islam et al., 2019), suggesting the polar side chain of cysteine likely disrupts the interaction network within the hydrophobic cluster.
evidence: Supported by citation to Islam et al., 2019.

claim: The polar side chain of cysteine in the W308C mutation likely disrupts the interaction network within the hydrophobic cluster of LKB1.
source: The W308C mutation has previously been identified to cause a reduction in LKB1 stability when compared to the wt variant (Islam et al., 2019), suggesting the polar side chain of cysteine likely disrupts the interaction network within the hydrophobic cluster.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural considerations.

claim: The LKB1 mutant W308C diminishes its catalytic activity.
source: Additionally, the LKB1 mutant W308C diminishes its catalytic activity (Islam et al., 2019, Boudeau et al., 2004, Mehenni et al., 1998), consistent with the observed prevention of the PPI-directed closing of the LKB1 KinCon reporter conformation (Figure 2I).
evidence: Supported by citations to Islam et al., 2019, Boudeau et al., 2004, and Mehenni et al., 1998, and experimental data in Figure 2I.

claim: LKB1-W308C lost its ability to form the heterotrimeric complex, with implications on hindering downstream activation and thus affecting its tumor suppressor functions.
source: These findings suggest that LKB1-W308C lost its ability to form the heterotrimeric complex, with implications on hindering downstream activation and thus affecting its tumor suppressor functions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: In contrast to the previously published MEK1 and BRAF KinCon reporter, the more closed STRADα and LKB1 KinCon reporter conformations represent the more active full-length kinase states.
source: Overall these findings underline that the KinCon technology can be extended to track the impact of binary protein complexes and related cancer mutations on kinase activity dynamics. Moreover, this data demonstrated that in contrast to the previously published MEK1 and BRAF KinCon reporter (Fleischmann et al., 2021, Fleischmann et al., 2023, Röck et al., 2019, Mayrhofer et al., 2020), the more closed STRADα and LKB1 KinCon reporter conformations represent the more active full-length kinase states.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and comparison with previous studies.

claim: Genetic alterations of RIPK1 are linked to immune and autoinflammatory diseases.
source: Genetic alterations of RIPK1 are linked to immune and autoinflammatory diseases (Lalaoui et al., 2020, Tao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lalaoui et al., 2020 and Tao et al., 2020.

claim: Small molecule-mediated inhibition of RIPK1 kinase activity was shown to counteract the necroptotic phenotype in disease models.
source: Small molecule-mediated inhibition of RIPK1 kinase activity was shown to counteract the necroptotic phenotype in disease models (Tao et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tao et al., 2020.

claim: Both RIPK1 and RIPK3 KinCon reporters exhibit markedly reduced bioluminescence in the necroptotic cellular environment.
source: We showed that both KinCon reporters exhibit markedly reduced bioluminescence in the necroptotic cellular environment (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Both RIPK1 and RIPK3 kinases shift to a more opened ON state of the full-length protein upon pathway activation.
source: These results support the notion that both kinases shift to a more opened ON state of the full-length protein upon pathway activation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The RIPK1 KinCon reporter was not capable of auto-phosphorylation.
source: Our results showed that the RIPK1 KinCon reporter was not capable of auto-phosphorylation.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: In the presence of active flag-tagged RIPK1, trans-phosphorylation of the KinCon reporter hybrid proteins was evident.
source: In the presence of active flag-tagged RIPK1 however, trans-phosphorylation of the KinCon reporter hybrid proteins was evident (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Auto-phosphorylations at the positions S14, S15, and S166 have been shown to trigger downstream activation of RIPK1.
source: Auto-phosphorylations at the positions S14, S15, and S166 have been shown to trigger downstream activation (Laurien et al., 2020, Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Laurien et al., 2020 and Wang et al., 2018.

claim: Auto-phosphorylation events at S14/S15/S166 are critical for RIPK1 activation.
source: Auto-phosphorylation events have been described for the positions S14/S15/S166 (referred to as S14/15/166) and are critical for RIPK1 activation (Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021.

claim: In addition to the kinase-deficient mutant (K45A), all the phosphorylation mimetic (S14/15/166E) and phosphorylation preventing (S14/15/166A) mutations tested led to an opening of RIPK1 conformations.
source: Our KinCon findings unexpectedly demonstrated for RIPK1 that in addition to the kinase-deficient mutant (K45A) all the phosphorylation mimetic (S14/15/166E) and phosphorylation preventing (S14/15/166A) mutations tested led to an opening of RIPK1 conformations (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: All patient mutations tested (D324A/E/H and C601Y) led to an opening of RIPK1 conformations.
source: Again, we observed an opening of RIPK1 conformations with all mutations tested (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The mutations at position 324 affect the activity conformation of RIPK1 in addition to preventing caspase 8 cleavage.
source: This data supports the notion that in addition to preventing caspase 8 cleavage the mutations at position 324 affect the activity conformation of RIPK1.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: The C601Y substitution promotes RIPK1 opening.
source: The C601Y substitution promotes RIPK1 opening as well.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The kinase-deficient mutation (K45A) of the KinCon biosensor displayed the strongest opening of the enzyme conformation.
source: The kinase-deficient mutation (K45A) of the KinCon biosensor displayed the strongest opening of the enzyme conformation.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Application of both Necrostatin and GSK547 showed engagement with all the tested RIPK1 KinCon reporters.
source: Application of both compounds showed engagement with all the tested RIPK1 KinCon reporters tested.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: An increase of bioluminescence for all RIPK1 inhibitors was evident reflecting the closing of the full-length kinase conformation.
source: An increase of bioluminescence for all RIPK1 inhibitors was evident reflecting the closing of the full-length kinase conformation.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The phosphorylation mimetic (S14/15/166E) and phosphorylation preventing (S14/15/166A) KinCon reporters showed promotion of a more closed configuration when compared to the unrelated small molecule control, the MEK1 kinase inhibitor Cobimetinib.
source: Even the phosphorylation mimetic (S14/15/166E) and phosphorylation preventing (S14/15/166A) KinCon reporters showed these phenomena of promoting a more closed conﬁguration when compared to the unrelated small molecule control, the MEK1 kinase inhibitor Cobimetinib (Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Application of both allosteric kinase blockers alters the RIPK1 conformations and scaffolding functions of active and inactive RIPK1 protomers.
source: This data underlines that application of both allosteric kinase blockers alters the RIPK1 conformations and we assume scaffolding functions of active and inactive RIPK1 protomers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data with speculation about scaffolding functions.

claim: CDK4 and CDK6 exhibit proto-oncogenic properties that rely on the presence and interaction with regulatory proteins.

evidence: Supported by citations to Scheiblecker et al., 2020 and Eferl and Wagner, 2003.

claim: CDK6 functions as a chromatin-bound factor and transcriptional regulator, thereby promoting the initiation of tumorigenesis.

evidence: Supported by citations to Kollmann et al., 2013, Semczuk and Jakowicki, 2004, Scheicher et al., 2015, and Kollmann and Sexl, 2013.

claim: CDK4/6 activities are modulated by its molecular interaction partners, particularly cyclins and proteinogenic inhibitors.

evidence: Supported by citations to Goel et al., 2018, Giacinti and Giordano, 2006, and Ortega et al., 2002.

claim: CDK4/6 deregulation is caused by alterations of protein expression levels and/or by mutations within regulatory proteins.
source: CDK4/6 deregulation is caused by alterations of protein expression levels and/or by mutations within regulatory proteins.
evidence: This is a general statement about CDK4/6 deregulation mechanisms.

claim: The CDK4/6-cyclinD protein complex has been found to be hyperactivated in many cancers and therefore promote tumor growth.
source: The CDK4/6-cyclinD protein complex has been found to be hyperactivated in many cancers and therefore promote tumor growth (Choi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Choi et al., 2012.

claim: Efficient CDK4/6 inhibitors such as Palbocilicb, Ribociclib, and Abemaciclib are currently in clinical use against breast cancer.
source: Efficient CDK4/6 inhibitors such as Palbocilicb, Ribociclib, and Abemaciclib are currently in clinical use against breast cancer (Otto and Sicinski, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Otto and Sicinski, 2017.

claim: A major drawback of CDK4/6 inhibitor therapies is the emergence of drug resistance.
source: A major drawback of these therapies is the emergence of drug resistance (Fassl et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fassl et al., 2022.

claim: The development of precision medicine oriented polypharmacology therapies is one strategy to avoid the early advent of resistance to CDK4/6 inhibitors.
source: The development of precision medicine oriented polypharmacology therapies is one strategy to avoid the early advent of resistance (Álvarez-Fernández and Malumbres, 2020, Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Álvarez-Fernández and Malumbres, 2020 and Yang et al., 2017.

claim: Substitution of arginine at the position 31 of CDK6 with cysteine (R31C) alters the binding affinities for p16INK4a.
source: It is evident that substitution of arginine at the position 31 of CDK6 with cysteine (R31C) alters the binding affinities for p16INK4a. It forms two ionic interactions with p16INK4a residues D74 and D84, which are lost in the R31C mutant (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: R31 in CDK6 forms two ionic interactions with p16INK4a residues D74 and D84, which are lost in the R31C mutant.
source: It forms two ionic interactions with p16INK4a residues D74 and D84, which are lost in the R31C mutant (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Experimental data supports that the R31C mutation in CDK6 alters binding affinities for p16INK4a.
source: Experimental data further supports this notion (Rodríguez-Díez et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodríguez-Díez et al., 2014.

claim: A significant reduction of p16INK4a:CDK4/6 complex formation was observed when the respective R residues are mutated to C.
source: Using this cell-based PPI reporter we observed a significant reduction of p16INK4a:CDK4/6 complex formation when the respective R residues are mutated to C.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations using the PPI reporter.

claim: Integration of the P40L mutation in p16INK4a prevented complex formation with CDK4/6.
source: Integration of the P40L mutation in p16INK4a prevented complex formation as expected and further validates the reporter system applied (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: P16INK4a binding deficient CDK4 and CDK6 mutants exhibited a more opened conformation, as indicated by a decrease in bioluminescence.
source: The results showed that the reduced affinity for p16INK4a binding alters the conformations of both CDKs. P16INK4a binding deficient CDK4 and CDK6 mutants exhibited a more opened conformation, as indicated by a decrease in bioluminescence (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: No major effects of drug exposure on the dynamics of the four CDK KinCon reporters which showed different affinities for p16INK4a binding were detected upon exposure to three clinically applied CDK4/6 inhibitors.
source: Overall we could not detect any major effects of drug exposure on the dynamics of the four CDK KinCon reporters which showed different affinities for p16INK4a binding (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Breast cancer drugs which should bind to the active protein kinase did not induce full-length CDK4 and CDK6 conformational changes in the tested cell culture settings.
source: This data underlines that these breast cancer drugs which should bind to the active protein kinase did not induce full-length CDK4 and CDK6 conformational changes in the tested cell culture settings.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Type I inhibitors selectively bind to the active conformation of the kinase, characterized by DFG in and αC in.
source: Type I inhibitors selectively bind to the active conformation of the kinase, characterized by DFG in and αC in.
evidence: This is a definition of type I inhibitors based on established knowledge.

claim: Type I 1/2 inhibitors bind to the inactive state of the kinase, represented by DFG in and αC out.
source: Type I 1/2 inhibitors, on the other hand, bind to the inactive state of the kinase, represented by DFG in and αC out.
evidence: This is a definition of type I 1/2 inhibitors based on established knowledge.

claim: Type II inhibitors bind to the inactive kinase, where DFG is out and αC can be either in or out.
source: Type II inhibitors bind to the inactive kinase, where DFG is out and αC can be either in or out (Arter et al., 2022; Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is a definition of type II inhibitors based on established knowledge, supported by citation to Arter et al., 2022.

claim: Type III (allosteric) inhibitors bind adjacent to the ATP-binding pocket, enabling simultaneous binding of ATP and the inhibitor.
source: However, type III (allosteric) inhibitors deviate from this pattern. They bind adjacent to the ATP-binding pocket, enabling simultaneous binding of ATP and the inhibitor (Wu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2015.

claim: Alterations of KinCon activity conformations were observed upon changes of protein interactions and through type I 1/2 and type III inhibitor binding, but not type I inhibitors.
source: In this study we have observed alterations of KinCon activity conformations upon changes of protein interactions and through type I 1/2 and type III inhibitor binding (Figure 5A–C), but not type I inhibitors.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings shown in Figure 5A–C.

claim: For both kinases of the MAPK pathway, MEK1 and BRAF, the respective inhibitors affect primarily the active kinase conformation.
source: We have previously shown that for both kinases of the MAPK pathway, MEK1 and BRAF, the respective inhibitors affect primarily the active kinase conformation (Röck et al., 2019, Mayrhofer et al., 2020, Fleischmann et al., 2021, Fleischmann et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Röck et al., 2019, Mayrhofer et al., 2020, Fleischmann et al., 2021, and Fleischmann et al., 2023.

claim: Both BRAF-V600E and MEK1-K57E kinases which are activated through cancer patient mutations bind the respective kinase inhibitor, resulting in a change in the activity conformations.
source: Exemplarily we illustrate that both kinases which are activated through cancer patient mutations (BRAF-V600E and MEK1-K57E) bind the respective kinase inhibitor, resulting in a change in the activity conformations (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: For all tested RIPK1 activity conformations, the binding of allosteric RIPK1i promoted a closing of the RIPK1 conformation.
source: In contrast, it was of interest that for all tested RIPK1 activity conformations we observed that the binding of allosteric RIPK1i promoted a closing of the RIPK1 conformation.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: Inactive RIPK1 complexes are target of drug binding with feasible consequences on kinase scaffolding functions.
source: This observation underlines that also inactive RIPK1 complexes are target of drug binding with feasible consequences on kinase scaffolding functions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claim: Reducing binding affinities for p16INK4a and related inhibitory proteins triggers the opening of the CDK6 KinCon.
source: We showed that reducing binding affinities for p16INK4a and related inhibitory proteins triggers the opening of the KinCon (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: None of the three clinically applied CDK4/6i tested (such as Abemaciclib) altered the kinase conformation significantly using the applied standard protocols for all CDK4/6 KinCon reporters.
source: However, using the applied standard protocols we have chosen for all CDK4/6 KinCon reporter we have not observed that any of the three clinically applied CDK4/6i tested (such as Abemaciclib) altered the kinase conformation significantly.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: When the regulatory (R) and the catalytic (C/PKAc) subunit interact, the tetrameric PKA holoenzyme complex (R2:C2) is inactive.
source: When the regulatory (R) and the catalytic (C/PKAc) subunit interact, the tetrameric PKA holoenzyme complex (R2:C2) is inactive.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about PKA regulation.

claim: Mutations such as L206R lock the catalytic subunit (PKAc) in its active state.
source: Mutations such as L206R lock the catalytic subunit (PKAc) in its active state.
evidence: This is a statement about the effect of the L206R mutation.

claim: Interactions of regulatory subunits with PKAc are significantly reduced by the L206R mutation.
source: Thus, interactions of regulatory subunits are significantly reduced (Mayrhofer et al., 2020, Bolger, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mayrhofer et al., 2020 and Bolger, 2022.

claim: Reduction of binding affinities through the use of the general cAMP elevating agent Forskolin triggers conformational changes to the more opened state of PKAc.
source: Reduction of binding affinities through the use of the general cAMP elevating agent Forskolin triggers conformational changes to the more opened state, mechanistically similar to CDK6-R31C.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations.

claim: The PKAc-L206R KinCon mutant already engages the opened activity conformation state.
source: The PKAc-L206R KinCon mutant already engages this opened activity conformation state (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Binary protein interactions are the prime factors for altering CDK4/6 and PKAc activity conformations.
source: Based on these two examples we assume that binary protein interactions are the prime factors for altering CDK4/6 and PKAc activity conformations.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Using PKAc and BRAF KinCon reporters, alterations of cytoplasmic and nuclear localization could not be tracked.
source: In the context of kinase compartmentalization and activating kinase mutations we showed that using PKAc and BRAF KinCon reporters as example we could not track alterations of cytoplasmic and nuclear localization (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Subcellular localization of PKAc KinCon reporters did not change when the L206R mutation was introduced.
source: Furthermore, subcellular localization of PKAc KinCon reporters did not change when the L206R mutation was introduced (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only a limited number of human kinases are targeted by approved drugs.
source: In this regard it is important to note that only a limited number of human kinases are targeted by approved drugs.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of kinase drug development.

claim: Numerous protein kinases lack drug candidates.
source: It is evident that numerous protein kinases lack drug candidates.
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of kinase drug development.

claim: Many kinases lack suitable tools/readouts for basic research analyses of physiological and pathological kinase functions.
source: Many of these miss suitable tools/readouts for basic research analyses of physiological and pathological kinase functions.
evidence: This is a general statement about the challenges in kinase research.

claim: Such kinases have been referred to be part of the so-called 'dark kinome'.
source: Such kinases have been referred to be part of the so-called 'dark kinome' (Berginski et al., 2021, Southekal et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berginski et al., 2021 and Southekal et al., 2021.

claim: KinCon reporters represent an extendable toolbox for gaining first and also deeper insights into alterations of kinase activity-related conformation states induced by different means of inhibitors, activators, binders, or mutations.
source: These conformation reporters represent an extendable toolbox for gaining first and also deeper insights into alterations of kinase activity-related conformation states induced by different means of inhibitors, activators, binders, or mutations.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the KinCon technology.

claim: Systematic implementation of KinCon technology in kinase research programs would assist in advancing our understanding of kinase and pseudokinase regulations and functions.
source: Systematic implementation of this technology in kinase research programs would assist in advancing our understanding of kinase and pseudokinase regulations and functions.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the KinCon technology.

claim: Despite significant efforts, only a small fraction of the entire kinome has been successfully targeted by FDA-approved kinase blockers so far.
source: Despite significant efforts in this direction, only a small fraction of the entire kinome has been successfully targeted by FDA-approved kinase blockers so far (Lahiry et al., 2010, Politi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lahiry et al., 2010 and Politi et al., 2015.

claim: Once a kinase inhibitor is introduced into clinical use, it often encounters the development of drug resistance mechanisms over time.
source: Moreover, once a kinase inhibitor is introduced into clinical use, it often encounters the development of drug resistance mechanisms over time (Longley and Johnston, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Longley and Johnston, 2005.

claim: It is crucial to gain more extensive insights into the cellular drug-target engagement, the molecular consequences of kinase patient mutations, and the evolving patterns of drug resistance mechanisms.
source: Hence, it is crucial to gain more extensive insights into the cellular drug-target engagement, the molecular consequences of kinase patient mutations, and the evolving patterns of drug resistance mechanisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of understanding kinase biology for therapeutic purposes.

claim: Anticipating and unveiling the cellular mechanism of drug actions may help to develop new treatment concepts with the hope of reducing the diminishing of drug efficacies.
source: Anticipating and unveiling the cellular mechanism of drug actions may help to develop new treatment concepts with the hope of reducing the diminishing of drug efficacies (Chan and Ginsburg, 2011, Goetz and Schork, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chan and Ginsburg, 2011 and Goetz and Schork, 2018.

claim: The KinCon technology has the potential to track kinase functions in living cells effectively, providing assistance in measuring difficult-to-assess processes that may include or go beyond phosphotransferase activities.
source: It has the potential to track kinase functions in living cells effectively, providing assistance in measuring difficult-to-assess processes that may include or go beyond phosphotransferase activities.
evidence: This is a statement about the capabilities of the KinCon technology.

claim: The KinCon technology offers an innovative solution for understanding kinase activity conformations, which could pave the way for new intervention strategies for kinase entities that have so far not been addressable for drug screenings.
source: Overall, it offers an innovative solution for understanding kinase activity conformations, which could pave the way for new intervention strategies for kinase entities that have so far not been addressable for drug screenings.
evidence: This is a statement about the potential impact of the KinCon technology.

claim: The KinCon technology relates to the tracking of kinase scaffold and pseudokinase functions.
source: So far, this relates to the tracking of kinase scaffold and pseudokinase functions.
evidence: This is a statement about the applications of the KinCon technology.

source: Key advantages of the KinCon reporter technology is the robustness of the system to track kinase conformations at varying expression levels.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the KinCon technology.

source: However, in contrast to fluorescence-based reporter readouts, subcellular analyses and cell sorting are still challenging due to comparably low levels of light emission.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the KinCon technology.

claim: Tracking enzyme activities at low expression levels is paramount for understanding the details of cellular functions, as many regulatory and spatiotemporal controlled kinase interactions occur under such settings.
source: Tracking enzyme activities at low expression levels is paramount for understanding the details of cellular functions, as many regulatory and spatiotemporal controlled kinase interactions occur under such settings.
evidence: This is a statement about the importance of tracking kinase activities at physiological expression levels.

claim: It is more challenging to identify activator molecules for promoting reactivation of the LKB1-AMPK axis in contrast to blockers of kinase functions.
source: In contrast to blockers of kinase functions it is more challenging to identify activator molecules for promoting reactivation of the LKB1-AMPK axis.

claim: Pseudokinases are more than inert scaffolds and are involved in modulating interacting enzyme entities.

claim: Pseudokinases can employ switch-like transitions to regulate signaling networks.

claim: There is a growing interest in exploring strategies to therapeutically restore the function of mutated LKB1 given the discovery of LKB1 inactivating mutations in diseases like PJS, NSCLC, and colorectal cancer.
source: Given the discovery of LKB1 inactivating mutations in diseases like PJS, NSCLC, and colorectal cancer, there is a growing interest in exploring strategies to therapeutically restore the function of mutated LKB1 (Sanchez-Cespedes, 2007, Launonen, 2005, Kitajima et al., 2019).

source: Functioning as a molecular scaffold, RIPK1 orchestrates signal transduction by coordinating multiple kinases participating in the NFκB pathway (Moynagh, 2005, Meylan et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moynagh, 2005 and Meylan et al., 2004.

claim: As a regulator of cell death, RIPK1 forms a substantial amyloid-like signalosome in conjunction with RIPK3 and various other factors.
source: Moreover, as a regulator of cell death, RIPK1 forms a substantial amyloid-like signalosome in conjunction with RIPK3 and various other factors (Degterev et al., 2019).

source: It needs to be noted that additional kinases have been linked to control the phosphorylation and activity state of RIPK1 (Dondelinger et al., 2019, Xu et al., 2018, Jaco et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dondelinger et al., 2019, Xu et al., 2018, and Jaco et al., 2017.

claim: K45 in RIPK1 corresponds to K78 in LKB1, highlighting the importance of this lysine residue in the functionality of various kinases.
source: Interestingly, K45 in RIPK1 corresponds to K78 in LKB1, highlighting the importance of this lysine residue in the functionality of various kinases.
